anchor_text: Sad, high, and working, full of state and woe
summary: 'Sad' here means serious, grave (not unhappy). 'Working' means powerfully affecting the emotions — the kind of drama that moves an audience to tears. The Prologue is warning that this play will be solemn and emotionally intense, not light entertainment.
detail: The Elizabethan sense of 'sad' (Old English saed, 'sated, weary, grave') as 'grave, serious' persisted well into the seventeenth century. 'Full of state' means concerned with matters of high government. 'Working' in the sense of emotionally operative or effective is recorded from the 1580s. Together the three adjectives stake out the play's generic claim: this is history drama in the de casibus mode, not comedy.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'sad' adj., sense 5: 'Grave, serious, sober'; s.v. 'working' adj., sense 3: 'Having a powerful effect on the mind or feelings.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 3
OED s.v. 'sad' sense 5 ('grave, serious') and s.v. 'working' sense 3 ('having a powerful effect on the mind or feelings') are real entries and accurately support the gloss on both words.

'Sad' meaning grave/serious and 'working' meaning emotionally effective are both well-attested Elizabethan senses, and the reading of the Prologue as staking a generic claim to solemn history is mainstream and supportable from the lines themselves.

anchor_text: come to hear a merry bawdy play, A noise of targets, or to see a fellow In a long motley coat
summary: The Prologue is ruling out three popular types of entertainment: a 'merry bawdy play' (a comedy full of sexual jokes), a stage battle with clanging shields ('targets'), and a 'motley coat' — the parti-coloured patched costume worn by the traditional stage clown or fool. The audience is told this play will offer none of those pleasures.
detail: A 'target' was a small round shield; the 'noise of targets' refers to the percussive sound of stage combats that audiences enjoyed as spectacle. The 'long motley coat guarded with yellow' is an exact description of the professional fool's stage costume — a long coat of mixed colours ('motley') trimmed with yellow ribbon or braid ('guarded'). Yellow was associated with folly and jealousy in Elizabethan costume convention. The Prologue is addressing audience expectations shaped by the popular theatre of the 1590s-1610s: clown shows, sword-fights, and bawdy comedy. Henry VIII offers instead 'chosen truth' — historically grounded tragedy.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'target' n.1, sense 3: 'A small round shield'; s.v. 'motley' n., sense 2: 'The parti-coloured coat of a jester.'

sources.name: Wiles, Shakespeare's Clown
sources.citation: David Wiles, Shakespeare's Clown: Actor and Text in the Elizabethan Playhouse (Cambridge UP, 1987), pp. 1-23, on the motley costume tradition.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 14

OED entries for 'target' (small round shield) and 'motley' (parti-coloured jester's coat) are real and supportive; Wiles, Shakespeare's Clown (Cambridge UP, 1987) is a real book that discusses the motley costume tradition in its opening chapters.

The three categories (bawdy comedy, stage combat, clown in motley) are correctly identified as popular genres the Prologue explicitly rejects, and 'guarded with yellow' as trim detail on the fool's costume is supported by the text itself.

anchor_text: then, in a moment, see How soon this mightiness meets misery
summary: The Prologue announces the play's central pattern: great men at the summit of power brought suddenly to ruin. This is the classic 'fall of princes' (de casibus) model of tragedy, and it applies to all three of the play's main losers — Buckingham, Wolsey, and Queen Katherine.
detail: The de casibus tradition runs from Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium (c. 1360) through Lydgate's Fall of Princes and A Mirror for Magistrates — a genre of warning tales in which Fortune's wheel spins the mighty downward. The Prologue's promise of 'mightiness meeting misery' primes the audience to read each fall that follows not as a random disaster but as a moral exemplum. The three-fold structure of the play — Buckingham destroyed in Act 2, Wolsey stripped in Act 3, Katherine dying in Act 4 — repeats the pattern three times, a rhythmic insistence unusual even within the genre.

sources.name: Boccaccio, De Casibus
sources.citation: Giovanni Boccaccio, De Casibus Virorum Illustrium (c. 1360); John Lydgate, Fall of Princes (1431-38); A Mirror for Magistrates (1559).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 29

Boccaccio's De Casibus Virorum Illustrium (c. 1360), Lydgate's Fall of Princes (1431-38), and A Mirror for Magistrates (1559) are all real works in the de casibus tradition and accurately support the claim.

The de casibus reading of the Prologue's pattern is the dominant critical consensus, and the three-fall structure (Buckingham, Wolsey, Katherine) is a defensible description of the play's architecture, though scholars debate whether Katherine's is a true 'fall.'

anchor_text: Those suns of glory, those two lights of men, Met in the vale of Andren
summary: Buckingham is referring to Henry VIII and the French king Francis I, who met in June 1520 at a location between the English-held town of Guines and the French town of Ardres — the event known as the Field of the Cloth of Gold. 'Vale of Andren' is 'the valley of Andres.' Buckingham was too ill with fever to attend.
detail: The summit took place in a valley between the English-controlled Pale of Calais and French territory. 'Andren' is an anglicized form of Ardres. The description of the two kings as 'suns of glory' uses the same solar imagery of majesty that Shakespeare employs across the history plays (see Holinshed's account of the meeting). Both kings were in their late twenties, athletic, splendidly dressed competitors who staged tournaments and wrestling alongside diplomatic banqueting.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the Field of the Cloth of Gold, June 1520.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 40

Holinshed's Chronicles (1587) does cover the Field of the Cloth of Gold (June 1520) and Henry VIII's meeting with Francis I in the vale between Guines and Ardres; the historical and textual claim is well-grounded.

'Vale of Andren' as a garbled 'Ardres' and the two kings as Henry and Francis at the Field of the Cloth of Gold (June 1520) is historically uncontroversial; the solar imagery of kings is well-established in the histories.

anchor_text: Made Britain India: every man that stood Show'd like a mine
summary: To Elizabethans 'India' meant fabulous wealth — gold, jewels, spice. Norfolk is saying that when the English contingent dressed in gold cloth, England itself seemed to become the richest place on earth: every courtier glittered like an open vein of ore ('a mine'). The comparison packs in the era's obsession with New World and Eastern riches.
detail: 'India' in this period could refer to the East Indies (the Spice Islands) or the West Indies, both associated with legendary treasure. 'Showed like a mine' — appeared to be a gold or silver mine — continues the metaphor of human bodies as geological deposits of wealth. The image captures the competitive display at the Field of the Cloth of Gold, where both nations spent ruinously on clothing and pageantry.

Schmidt's Shakespeare-Lexicon entry for 'India' as a type of fabulous wealth is real and supportive; Holinshed (1587) does record the extravagant expenditure on cloth-of-gold at the 1520 summit.
'India' as the Elizabethan byword for fabulous wealth is standard, and 'showed like a mine' as a gold-or-silver-mine image is the plain sense of the lines.

anchor_text: their very labour Was to them as a painting. Now this masque Was cried incomparable
summary: 'Painting' here means cosmetics — the sweat of the overdressed ladies made them flushed, which served as a natural blush. A 'masque' is an elaborate courtly entertainment combining dance, music, costume, and allegorical spectacle, not the painted face-covering. 'Cried incomparable' means proclaimed by all to be without equal.
detail: The comparison of sweat to 'painting' (face-paint, cosmetics) is a witty backhanded compliment: their physical effort gave the noblewomen a natural flush that complemented their heavy court dress. 'Masque' (also spelled 'mask') was the quintessential Jacobean court entertainment — Ben Jonson and Inigo Jones were its masters; Shakespeare's company performed in several. At the Field of the Cloth of Gold, masques and pageants were staged every evening. 'Cried' = proclaimed, announced aloud.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'masque' n., sense 2: 'An elaborate courtly entertainment or dramatic composition with music, singing, and dancing.' Also s.v. 'painting' n., sense 5: 'The use of cosmetics.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 62
OED s.v. 'masque' (elaborate courtly entertainment) and s.v. 'painting' (use of cosmetics) are real entries that support both glosses; no overreach in the claims.

'Painting' as cosmetics and the reading that the ladies' flush from exertion served as a natural blush-paint is the standard editorial gloss; 'masque' as court entertainment is correctly distinguished from a face-mask.

anchor_text: former fabulous story, Being now seen possible enough, got credit, That Bevis was believ'd
summary: Bevis of Hampton was the hero of a popular medieval English romance, famous for superhuman feats of strength and knightly combat so extreme they were dismissed as fiction. Norfolk is saying the knights at the Field of the Cloth of Gold performed so spectacularly in the jousts that the impossible deeds of old romances suddenly seemed believable by comparison — the real world had caught up with legend.
detail: Bevis of Hampton (Bevis of Southampton) was one of the most beloved of the medieval English romances, still being printed in the early seventeenth century; Bevis slays giants, a dragon, and armies of Saracens. The allusion clusters this event with Arthurian or chivalric legend. The joke is that eyewitness reality was so astonishing it validated what had seemed mythological. It also subtly places the Field of the Cloth of Gold in the discourse of romance and spectacle — show without substance, the theme of the scene.

sources.name: Bullough, Narrative and Dramatic Sources
sources.citation: Geoffrey Bullough, Narrative and Dramatic Sources of Shakespeare, vol. 4 (Routledge, 1962), pp. 449-50, on the Bevis allusion in the Field of the Cloth of Gold narrative.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 73

Bullough's Narrative and Dramatic Sources vol. 4 (1962) does cover Henry VIII and the Bevis allusion is discussed in the scholarly literature, but the specific page range 449-50 cannot be independently verified from available sources.

Bevis of Hampton as a medieval romance hero famous for superhuman feats is correct, and the interpretive point — that the real spectacle made legendary fiction plausible — follows directly from the lines.

anchor_text: One, certes, that promises no element In such a business
summary: 'Certes' is an archaic adverb meaning 'certainly, assuredly' — a formal affirmation used ironically here. Norfolk is saying the event was organized by someone who (at first glance) seems completely unsuited to it — before revealing it was Cardinal Wolsey. The pause before naming him heightens the political tension.
detail: 'Certes' (from Old French certes, Latin certe) was already archaic and slightly elevated in tone by the Jacobean period, lending Norfolk's response a courtly formality. 'Promises no element' means 'gives no sign of any natural part or fitness' — 'element' in the sense of a person's natural sphere or domain. The construction builds suspense: who could be less expected to orchestrate a chivalric summit than a cardinal who rose from butcher-shop origins?

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'certes' adv.: 'Certainly, assuredly; in truth' (archaic by the 17th century).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 87
OED s.v. 'certes' ('certainly, assuredly; archaic by the 17th century') is a real entry that accurately supports the archaic adverb gloss.

'Certes' as a formal affirmation and 'promises no element' as 'gives no sign of natural fitness' are the accepted readings; the suspense-building irony before the reveal of Wolsey is clearly supported by the dialogue.

anchor_text: such a keech can with his very bulk Take up the rays o' th' beneficial sun, And keep it from the earth
summary: A 'keech' is a lump of rolled-up fat from a slaughtered animal — a butcher's term. It is a savage insult aimed at Wolsey, whose father was actually a butcher in Ipswich: Buckingham is calling him a greasy lump of tallow so massive that his bulk blocks sunlight (the king's favor) from reaching the land (the nobility). The image reduces Wolsey from a churchman to a piece of meat.
detail: The word 'keech' appears in 2 Henry IV as well (2.1), where Hostess Quickly calls Falstaff a 'keech' — suggesting it was current London slang for a fat-roll of suet. Wolsey's origins as the son of an Ipswich butcher were a constant point of aristocratic contempt: the nobles resented being outranked by a 'low-born' clergyman. The solar imagery (the king as sun) appears across Shakespeare's history plays as standard monarchical metaphor; here Buckingham's complaint is that Wolsey stands between the nobility and the royal light.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'keech' n.: 'A lump of fat rolled up by a butcher'; recorded from the 1590s.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 95

OED s.v. 'keech' ('a lump of fat rolled up by a butcher') is real and supportive; Holinshed (1587) does record Wolsey's father as a butcher of Ipswich, and the annotation does not overreach either source.

'Keech' as a lump of butcher's fat is well-established, Wolsey's father's occupation as a butcher is historical fact, and the solar king-metaphor (sun blocked by Wolsey's bulk) is unambiguous in the lines.

anchor_text: being not propp'd by ancestry, whose grace Chalks successors their way, nor call'd upon For high feats done to the crown; neither allied To eminent assistants; but, spider-like, Out of his self-drawing web, he gives us note
summary: Norfolk explains how Wolsey rose without the usual advantages of noble birth, inherited connections, military achievement, or powerful relatives — and compares him to a spider spinning its own web out of its own body ('self-drawing'). Wolsey's power comes entirely from his own ability, which is both what makes him impressive and what the nobility finds threatening.
detail: The speech accurately captures the unusual social trajectory of Thomas Wolsey (c. 1473-1530): he had no hereditary title, no military record, no noble patrons — he rose through the Church by sheer administrative genius and royal favor. The spider-web image ('self-drawing web') is double-edged: spiders were associated with industry and ingenuity but also with predatory entrapment and deceit. 'Chalks successors their way' uses the image of chalk lines drawn on a road to guide travelers — ancestry as a visible path. The passage is drawn from Holinshed's characterization of Wolsey's rise.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Wolsey's origin and rise to power.

sources.name: Cavendish, Life of Wolsey
sources.citation: George Cavendish, The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey (written c. 1554-57), chapter 1, on Wolsey's beginnings in the church.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 100

Holinshed (1587) and Cavendish's Life of Wolsey (written c. 1554-57, the date range is accurate) both document Wolsey's self-made rise, and the annotation's claims are squarely within what those sources report.

The spider/self-drawing-web image as double-edged (industrious yet predatory) and 'chalks successors their way' as the chalk-road metaphor are defensible and mainstream; the description of Wolsey's rise without hereditary advantage is historically accurate.

anchor_text: If not from hell, the devil is a niggard, Or has given all before, and he begins A new hell in himself
summary: Abergavenny says Wolsey's pride is so extreme that if it did not come from Hell, then the devil must be a miser — he has given everything he had, all at once, to Wolsey — or Wolsey has gone so far he has created his own private hell inside himself. The implication is that Wolsey's pride is literally diabolical: the same sin that made Satan fall from heaven.
detail: Christian theology, following Isaiah 14:12 and Revelation 12, identified pride as the sin of Lucifer — the angel who fell from heaven because he exalted himself. By having Abergavenny trace Wolsey's pride to the devil, the play anticipates the Cardinal's own later self-diagnosis: 'Cromwell, I charge thee, fling away ambition: / By that sin fell the angels' (3.2). The image of a 'new hell' in the self also echoes the Miltonic tradition of the self-enclosed, self-damned sinner. 'Niggard' means a miser.

sources.name: Geneva Bible 1599
sources.citation: Isaiah 14:12 (Geneva 1599): 'How art thou fallen from heauen, O Lucifer, sonne of the morning!'; Revelation 12:9 (the fall of Satan and his angels).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 112

Geneva Bible (1599) Isaiah 14:12 ('How art thou fallen from heauen, O Lucifer, sonne of the morning!') and Revelation 12:9 are real verses whose content supports the identification of pride as the sin of Lucifer.

The biblical allusion to Lucifer's fall from pride is a sound general reading, but the annotation reaches in claiming anticipation of Wolsey's 3.2 'by that sin fell the angels' speech and invoking 'Miltonic tradition' — Milton's Paradise Lost postdates this play by fifty years and cannot be a meaningful parallel; the core gloss is defensible but the comparative apparatus overreaches.

anchor_text: Without the privity o' the King, to appoint Who should attend on him? He makes up the file Of all the gentry
summary: 'Privity' means private knowledge or consent — acting 'without the privity of the King' means doing something behind the king's back. 'Makes up the file' means draws up the list (a 'file' was a string on which papers were threaded, hence any ordered roster). Buckingham accuses Wolsey of unilaterally deciding who would accompany Henry to France without royal authorization.
detail: The complaint is historically grounded: contemporaries did accuse Wolsey of managing the selection of the nobles who attended the Field of the Cloth of Gold, allegedly burdening those he disliked with ruinously expensive requirements while giving easy assignments to his allies. Holinshed records the resentment. 'Privity' (from Latin privatus) carries its legal sense of private authorization or knowledge; to act without a superior's privity was to exceed one's authority.

'Privity' as private consent or knowledge and 'file' as an ordered list of names are both accurately glossed, and the historical charge that Wolsey controlled appointments for the French expedition is supported by Holinshed.

anchor_text: Have broke their backs with laying manors on 'em For this great journey
summary: To 'lay a manor on' someone means to stake an entire landed estate — a manor house and its associated lands — as the cost of participation. Buckingham is saying nobles were financially ruined by what it cost to outfit themselves, their retinues, and their equipment for the Field of the Cloth of Gold to Wolsey's standard. The event was literally bankrupting.
detail: Holinshed and contemporary accounts confirm that many English nobles spent catastrophically on the 1520 summit. The requirement to appear in gold-threaded cloth, maintain large retinues, and fund weeks of feasting drained estates that had taken generations to build. 'Manor' as a unit of wealth — the basic building-block of English aristocratic property — makes the image concrete: whole estates were pledged or sold. This is the first of many moments in the play where the gap between brilliant show and lasting substance is made literal in financial terms.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the financial ruin brought on nobles by the 1520 French expedition.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 129
Holinshed (1587) does record that English nobles were financially ruined by the cost of the 1520 Field of the Cloth of Gold; the claim is historically grounded in the cited source.

The idiom 'lay a manor on' as staking an entire estate and the historical confirmation of ruinous expenditure at the Field of the Cloth of Gold are correct; the broader thematic point about show versus substance is well grounded in the scene.

anchor_text: A thing inspir'd; and, not consulting, broke Into a general prophecy, that this tempest, Dashing the garment of this peace, aboded The sudden breach on't
summary: 'A thing inspired' means someone seized by prophetic impulse — as if a divine spirit had entered them. 'Not consulting' = without deliberating, spontaneously. 'Aboded' means 'portended, foretold' (to 'abode' something was to predict it as an omen). Buckingham is saying that after the violent storm that struck on the day of the peace ceremony, everyone was suddenly seized with a conviction — like prophecy — that the storm was an omen that the peace treaty would break.
detail: The storm at the Field of the Cloth of Gold is historically attested: Holinshed records that on the final day, a sudden violent tempest destroyed many of the tents and pavilions, which contemporaries interpreted as an ill omen. To be 'inspired' in this period could mean literally 'breathed into' by a spirit — divine, prophetic, or demonic. The political upshot is that the peace between England and France was indeed short-lived; within two years Henry allied with the Emperor against France.

sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the storm at the close of the Field of the Cloth of Gold.

Holinshed (1587) does record a violent storm at the close of the Field of the Cloth of Gold and its ominous reception; OED s.v. 'abode' v. sense 2 ('to forebode, portend') is a real archaic entry supporting the gloss.

'Inspired' as seized by a spirit (literally 'breathed into'), 'not consulting' as acting without deliberation, and 'aboded' as portended are standard glosses; the historical storm at the close of the Field of the Cloth of Gold is attested.

anchor_text: France hath flaw'd the league, and hath attach'd Our merchants' goods at Bordeaux
summary: 'Flaw'd the league' means cracked, broken the treaty — 'flaw' means a crack or split, used here as a verb. 'Attached' means legally seized, arrested (a legal term for confiscating property or detaining a person). France has broken the peace agreement and legally impounded English merchants' goods in Bordeaux as an act of economic warfare.
detail: 'Flaw' as a verb meaning to crack or break was in common use; the image of a treaty as something that can develop a 'flaw' (a structural crack, like in a gem or timber) is precise. 'Attach' in the legal sense of seizure continues the play's pattern of using law's vocabulary — arrest, attach, warrant — to describe political violence. The confiscation of English merchants' goods at Bordeaux (a major wine-trading port) would have been economically damaging and practically felt by London merchants.

'Flaw'd' as cracked or broken and 'attach'd' in the legal sense of seizure are accurate; Bordeaux as an English wine-trading port where confiscation would have immediate commercial impact is correctly contextualised.

anchor_text: Marry, is't
summary: 'Marry' is a mild oath, a shortened form of 'Mary' — an invocation of the Virgin Mary. By Shakespeare's time it had faded to a general exclamation meaning something like 'indeed' or 'of course.' Norfolk is confirming: 'Yes, that's exactly why.'
detail: Such oaths by the Virgin's name — 'Mary,' 'Marry,' 'By Our Lady' — were pervasive in pre-Reformation English speech and survived as empty expletives long after the Reformation stripped them of devotional content. The 1606 Act to Restrain Abuses of Players prohibited profane oaths on stage using the names of God or Christ; invoking Mary was legal. 'Marry' appears dozens of times across the Shakespeare canon as a conversational filler.

OED s.v. 'marry' int. (exclamation derived from the name of the Virgin Mary) is a real entry that accurately supports the gloss.
'Marry' as a vestigial oath derived from Mary (the Virgin) that had faded to a conversational affirmative by this period is standard, and the note on the 1606 Act is relevant and accurate.

anchor_text: Bosom up my counsel
summary: To 'bosom up' counsel means to store it in your breast — to take advice to heart and keep it close, as if you were hiding it in the folds of your garment. Norfolk is urging Buckingham to treasure and act on his warning about Wolsey privately, not to trumpet his grievances aloud.
detail: 'Bosom' as a verb meaning to hide or cherish in the breast (used figuratively for the heart and inner self) appears rarely but is recorded from the early seventeenth century. The physical image is of tucking a paper or an object into the fold of the doublet against the chest — a gesture of concealment and safekeeping. The counsel Norfolk wants Buckingham to 'bosom up' is the warning not to antagonize Wolsey publicly.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 164
OED s.v. 'bosom' v. sense 1 ('to conceal in the bosom; to hide, keep secret') is a real entry that accurately supports the archaic verb gloss.
'Bosom up' as to conceal or cherish secretly in the breast is the accepted meaning, and the physical image of tucking something into the doublet follows naturally from the figurative usage.

anchor_text: This butcher's cur is venom-mouth'd, and I Have not the power to muzzle him; therefore best Not wake him in his slumber. A beggar's book Outworths a noble's blood
summary: Buckingham calls Wolsey a 'butcher's cur' — the vicious guard-dog of a butcher (whose father was literally a butcher). 'Venom-mouthed' means spitting poison. 'A beggar's book outworths a noble's blood' is Buckingham's bitter complaint that book-learning (Wolsey's route to power through the Church and the law) is now worth more than noble birth — the world is upside-down.
detail: Wolsey's father was an Ipswich butcher, and his opponents never let him forget it. 'Cur' was the standard term for a mixed-breed or worthless dog — hence a low, dangerous mongrel, not a proper hunting or lap dog. The line 'a beggar's book outworths a noble's blood' is Buckingham's aristocratic protest against meritocracy: the educated cleric can outrank the hereditary peer. This is historically pointed — Wolsey held the Lord Chancellorship, the highest legal office, by virtue of his administrative brilliance and royal favor, not by birth.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Wolsey's origins as the son of an Ipswich butcher.

sources.name: Cavendish, Life of Wolsey
sources.citation: George Cavendish, The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey (written c. 1554-57), on the nobles' resentment of Wolsey's origins.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 174
Holinshed (1587) and Cavendish's Life of Wolsey both document Wolsey's Ipswich butcher father and the aristocratic resentment it provoked; the annotation does not overreach either source.

'Cur' as a mongrel or low dog and 'a beggar's book outworths a noble's blood' as aristocratic protest against meritocracy are the standard readings; the annotation correctly identifies this as Buckingham's class-based complaint rather than a general anti-intellectualism.

anchor_text: let your reason with your choler question What 'tis you go about. To climb steep hills Requires slow pace at first
summary: 'Choler' was one of the four bodily humors — the hot, fiery yellow bile that was held to produce anger, rashness, and irritability. Norfolk is urging Buckingham to let his reason cross-examine his anger before he acts. The advice 'to climb steep hills requires slow pace at first' is a proverbial comparison: rushing at a steep climb exhausts you before you reach the top, just as rushing at Wolsey before you have a strategy will destroy you.
detail: In Galenic medicine, which governed Elizabethan understanding of the body, a surplus of yellow bile ('choler') made a person hot-tempered and impulsive. The four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) determined personality and health; a 'choleric' person was prone to anger and quick action. Norfolk's advice to let reason 'question' choler personifies the faculties as adversaries in a debate — the rhetoric of the period's psychology. The proverbial hill-climbing image is a commonplace of patience-literature.

anchor_text: Anger is like A full hot horse, who being allow'd his way, Self-mettle tires him
summary: Norfolk compares anger to a horse given free rein when it is at full heat ('full hot'): the horse's own energy, uncontrolled, will exhaust it. 'Self-mettle' means its own spirit or fire. The point is that Buckingham's fury, if unchecked, will wear itself out and destroy him before he can act effectively against Wolsey.

'Mettle' — courage, spirit, fire — was spelled interchangeably with 'metal,' keeping the sense of the horse's material temperament alive.

anchor_text: This Ipswich fellow's insolence, or proclaim There's difference in no persons
summary: Buckingham contemptuously calls Wolsey 'this Ipswich fellow' — Ipswich was the Suffolk market town where Wolsey was born, and naming him by his birthplace rather than his titles is a deliberate snub. 'There's difference in no persons' means 'there is no distinction of rank anymore' — if Wolsey can act this way, birth and title count for nothing.

For Buckingham — a Stafford, descendant of Edward III — to be governed by the son of an Ipswich butcher was a social abomination. 'There's difference in no persons' articulates the aristocratic fear that the Tudor meritocracy (churchmen, lawyers, merchants rising to power) was erasing the inherited hierarchy.

anchor_text: This holy fox, Or wolf, or both,--for he is equal ravenous As he is subtle, and as prone to mischief As able to perform't
summary: Buckingham piles up animal images for Wolsey: a 'holy fox' (a cunning deceiver who wears a religious disguise) or a 'wolf' (rapaciously devouring). The fox was the traditional image of sly cunning and hypocrisy; the wolf of predatory greed. Combining them ('or both') says Wolsey is simultaneously a clever hypocrite and a naked predator — he uses sanctity as cover for appetite.

A 'holy fox' — a fox who puts on holy airs — is the specific charge of religious hypocrisy against a cardinal. The wolf-devouring-the-flock (pastor/predator inversion) is equally biblical and proverbial. Both images build the extended beast-characterization of Wolsey that runs through the play, culminating in his own 'naked to mine enemies' image and in his comparison to fallen angels.

anchor_text: My lord the Duke of Buckingham, and Earl Of Hereford, Stafford, and Northampton, I Arrest thee of high treason, in the name Of our most sovereign king
summary: The Sergeant-at-Arms recites Buckingham's full titleage — Duke of Buckingham, Earl of Hereford, Stafford, and Northampton — before arresting him for high treason. The accumulation of titles makes the arrest more dramatic: all those ranks and honors are being brought down at once. Edward Stafford, the third Duke of Buckingham, was in fact arrested in April 1521 and executed in May on the testimony of his own discharged surveyor.

The historical Buckingham's conviction rested on the testimony of his dismissed estate surveyor, who claimed Buckingham had predicted that if Henry died childless the Stafford line (descended from Edward III's youngest son, Thomas of Woodstock) would inherit the throne. The surveyor's motive appears to have been personal grievance; Buckingham insisted the evidence was perjured. The arrest here, immediately after Buckingham has denounced Wolsey, completes the audience's understanding that the Cardinal has struck first.

anchor_text: The will of Heaven Be done in this and all things! I obey
summary: Buckingham's acceptance of his arrest in the words of the Lord's Prayer ('Thy will be done') establishes the first of the play's three de casibus exemplars in a Christian key. Rather than raging, he submits — modeling the patience under Fortune that the Prologue promised would be the play's theme. The same words are repeated by Abergavenny a few lines later, amplifying the effect.

It distinguishes the play's moral register from the tragic heroics of the Roman plays: dignity, not defiance, is the measure of the fallen great. The de casibus pattern is thus given its specifically Christian, providential form.

anchor_text: my life is spann'd already. I am the shadow of poor Buckingham, Whose figure even this instant cloud puts on, By dark'ning my clear sun

anchor_text: There have been commissions Sent down among 'em, which hath flaw'd the heart Of all their loyalties
summary: 'Commissions' here are royal writs authorizing the collection of a forced loan — a tax collected without parliamentary consent. Katherine is telling Henry that these writs, sent into the counties, have shattered ('flaw'd' = cracked, split) the people's loyalty. The episode reflects a real crisis: in 1525 Wolsey attempted to levy an extra-parliamentary 'Amicable Grant' of one-sixth of every subject's income to fund a war with France; it triggered near-rebellion in East Anglia and was quickly cancelled.

Shakespeare and Fletcher compress historical events here: Buckingham's arrest and the forced-loan crisis belong to different years (1521 and 1525), but placing them together sharpens the portrait of Wolsey's overreach.

summary: Henry says actions without precedent ('without example' = without a prior case to justify them) are dangerous in their results ('issue'). He is rebuking Wolsey's unauthorized commission: because there is no legal precedent for the levy, subjects rightly fear its consequences and resist. This is also a statement of Tudor constitutional doctrine — the king should act through established legal forms, not arbitrary orders.
detail: The principle resonates beyond the scene: the play's larger drama of the divorce (the 'King's Great Matter') turns precisely on whether Henry can act 'without example' in repudiating a papal dispensation and breaking with Rome. Henry here articulates a rule he will soon bend dramatically himself. The irony is available to the audience if not to the characters.

sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Henry VIII's revocation of the Amicable Grant on the grounds that it had been issued without proper authority.

The gloss on 'without example' as lacking legal precedent is sound, but the detail annotation's claim that Henry's words here foreshadow his own future breach of precedent in the divorce (the 'Great Matter') is a thematic interpretation the scene itself cannot support — Henry has no knowledge of future events, and imposing retrospective dramatic irony as though it were available to the audience at this moment is a speculative directorial reading, not a textual one; flag for h

anchor_text: From every tree lop, bark, and part o' the timber; And, though we leave it with a root, thus hack'd, The air will drink the sap
summary: Henry extends the forced-levy into a vivid image of destructive tree-pruning: if you strip the bark and outer wood from every tree yet leave the root, the exposed tree will still die — the air draws out the sap through the wounds. He is arguing that taking one-sixth of a subject's substance damages the whole organism of the kingdom, even if it does not kill it outright. The tree image implies that governance depends on not stripping the subjects who sustain it.

anchor_text: Let there be letters writ to every shire, Of the King's grace and pardon. The grieved commons Hardly conceive of me; let it be nois'd That through our intercession this revokement And pardon comes
summary: In a whispered aside to his secretary while the king speaks publicly of free pardon, Wolsey quietly appropriates the credit for himself. He tells the secretary to circulate news ('let it be nois'd') that the revocation comes through Wolsey's own intercession, not the king's mercy. 'Hardly conceive of me' means the commons think badly of him; he is trying to repair his reputation by stealing the king's benevolence. The stage direction marks the aside as meant for the audience, not the king.
detail: The maneuver is historically attested: Holinshed notes that Wolsey attempted to take credit for the cancellation of the Amicable Grant. The scene dramatizes his chronic political vice — even in retreat, he reaches for personal advantage. Katherine will see through it (her silence at this moment is telling), and the audience sees the full hypocrisy: within thirty lines of Katherine's public accusation that he is the 'putter on' of these exactions, he is privately claiming credit for their cancellation.

The stage direction explicitly marks this as an aside to the Secretary, and Wolsey's maneuver — appropriating royal credit for the pardon — is exactly what the lines say; Holinshed's attestation of Wolsey's attempt to take credit for the Grant's cancellation further confirms the reading.

anchor_text: This man so complete, Who was enroll'd 'mongst wonders
summary: 'Complete' here means accomplished in every virtue — not merely finished but fully and perfectly formed in all admirable qualities. To be 'enroll'd 'mongst wonders' means to be listed or recorded among extraordinary people, counted among marvels. Henry is saying that Buckingham was once universally acknowledged as a paragon — which makes his corruption all the more terrible.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'complete' adj. 4: fully endowed with all necessary or admirable qualities; 'enroll' v. 3: to enter in a list or record, to register among a number.

OED s.v. 'complete' adj. 4 records 'fully endowed with all admirable qualities' and s.v. 'enroll' v. 3 records 'to enter in a list or record'; both citations are real and support the gloss.

'Complete' as fully accomplished in all virtues and 'enroll'd 'mongst wonders' as counted among marvels are both standard Elizabethan senses well-attested in OED; the reading is precise and not inflated.

anchor_text: Hath into monstrous habits put the graces That once were his, and is become as black As if besmear'd in hell
summary: Henry uses the image of clothing to describe moral corruption: Buckingham has dressed his former virtues ('graces') in 'monstrous habits' — habits means both 'garments' and 'practices/customs,' so the word carries both senses at once. A man who was once fair is now as black as if smeared with the pitch and soot of hell. The de casibus pattern is visible: a man exalted by gifts falls when those gifts serve corruption.
detail: The 'black/besmear'd in hell' image draws on the conventional association of hell with darkness, fire, and pitch or sulphur — the smell of brimstone. 'Habits' exploiting the clothes/custom double meaning was a common rhetorical device; cf. Hamlet 1.4 ('the stamp of one defect... shall in the general censure take corruption'). The passage introduces the de casibus logic that structures the play's three great falls — Buckingham, Wolsey, and Katherine — each brought down at the height of gifts.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'habit' n. 4a: garment, costume; 4b: mental constitution, settled disposition — the double sense is exploited here.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 435

The 'habits' double meaning (garments / practices) is a genuine and well-documented rhetorical device in Elizabethan usage, and the de casibus pattern applied to Buckingham's fall is defensible; the Hamlet 1.4 parallel is apt but kept as a comparandum, not an over-claim.

anchor_text: a vain prophecy of Nicholas Henton
summary: Nicholas Hopkins (called 'Henton' in this edition after his Charterhouse at Henton in Somerset) was a real Carthusian monk who, according to Holinshed, fed Buckingham a series of prophecies about his future greatness and about the king dying without male heirs. A 'Chartreux friar' (TLN 467) is a Carthusian — a monk of the Order of the Chartreuse, famous for strict silence and seclusion. That such a man would 'feed' a duke with royal prophecies made the testimony doubly damning at trial.
detail: Holinshed records the monk's name as Hopkins and the house as the Charterhouse of Henton in Somerset. The Carthusian order (founded at the Grande Chartreuse, France) was known in England for its rigorous discipline; its members were among the most respected of the religious. That Buckingham's confessor was an apparently devout Carthusian gave the prophecies the color of spiritual authority, which is why they were so dangerous — and why the Surveyor's report of them is so damaging. Historically Hopkins was examined and the evidence used at Buckingham's 1521 trial.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 465

Holinshed (1587) records Nicholas Hopkins (called 'Henton' from the Charterhouse at Hinton in Somerset), his prophecies to Buckingham, and his role in the 1521 treason trial — all details in the annotation are confirmed by the chronicle.

The identification of Nicholas Hopkins / 'Henton' with the Charterhouse at Henton, Somerset, and the Carthusian order, is accurate and follows Holinshed; the annotation correctly notes the monk's name is Hopkins in Holinshed and 'Henton' in this edition without conflating them.

anchor_text: You were the Duke's surveyor, and lost your office On the complaint o' the tenants
summary: Katherine delivers the scene's most penetrating moment of skepticism: she reminds the court that the Surveyor was Buckingham's estate-manager who was fired after his own tenants complained about him. A 'surveyor' was a manorial officer who assessed, managed, and collected rents from an estate — a position of considerable local power. This man has an obvious grudge against his former master, and his testimony is correspondingly unreliable. Katherine is warning everyone that a disgraced ex-employee testifying against his lord is exactly the kind of 'spleen' (personal spite) that distorts truth.
detail: Holinshed confirms the detail: the Surveyor (historically Charles Knyvet) was dismissed by Buckingham after tenants complained, and his testimony was procured by Wolsey. Katherine's intervention is the only challenge to the Surveyor's credibility the scene offers, and Henry — notably — ignores it. The moment crystallizes her role in the play as the moral voice others will not hear: she is right about the Surveyor's motive, right about Wolsey's manipulation, and right that the king's justice is being manipulated. None of it saves Buckingham.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Charles Knyvet, Buckingham's surveyor, dismissed on tenants' complaints and subsequently providing evidence against his master at Wolsey's instigation.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 493

Holinshed (1587) confirms that the surveyor (historically Charles Knyvet) was dismissed by Buckingham after tenants complained and that his evidence against Buckingham was procured at Wolsey's instigation, supporting all historical claims in the annotation.

Katherine's challenge to the Surveyor's credibility is explicitly present in the lines she speaks, Holinshed confirms the Surveyor (Charles Knyvet) was dismissed on tenants' complaints, and characterizing her intervention as the scene's 'only challenge to credibility' is accurate — Henry immediately overrides her at TLN 498.

anchor_text: I would have play'd The part my father meant to act upon The usurper Richard; who, being at Salisbury, Made suit to come in 's presence; which if granted, As he made semblance of his duty, would Have put his knife into him
summary: Buckingham is reported boasting that if he had been imprisoned he would have done what his father planned: kill Richard III. The 'usurper Richard' is Richard III; 'at Salisbury' refers to a moment when the historical Henry Stafford, second Duke of Buckingham (father of this play's Duke), rebelled against Richard in 1483. The plan to request an audience and then assassinate Richard — the knife producing 'his duty' while really planning murder — is attested in Tudor chronicle as one of the plots against the usurper.
detail: Buckingham's father joined the rebellion against Richard III in 1483 and was captured and executed at Salisbury on 2 November 1483 before the plot could reach Henry Tudor. This play's Buckingham is thus the son of a man who died trying to overthrow a king, which makes his own reported boast — that he would pick up where his father left off — the most damning possible evidence of treasonous intent. The Surveyor's account makes the boast vivid with the gesture of the knife (TLN 526, 533) and the oath. Shakespeare and Fletcher draw the Salisbury episode from Holinshed's account of Richard III's reign.

sources.name: Holinshed
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the rebellion and execution of Henry Stafford, second Duke of Buckingham, at Salisbury, November 1483, during the reign of Richard III.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 521

Holinshed records the elder Buckingham's rebellion and execution at Salisbury (2 Nov 1483), but the specific detail of a plan to request an audience with Richard III at Salisbury and assassinate him with a knife is a dramatic elaboration from the play's Surveyor speech; no chronicle source clearly attests this plan as a premeditated knife-assassination request, so the claim that Holinshed directly supports this specific episode is unverified.

The identification of 'the usurper Richard' with Richard III and the reference to the elder Buckingham's 1483 rebellion and execution at Salisbury is historically accurate and follows Holinshed; the reading that the boast makes the son's treasonous intent maximally damning is well-grounded.

anchor_text: There's his period, To sheathe his knife in us. He is attach'd
summary: 'Period' here means the end-point, the full stop — the final purpose of everything the Surveyor has described. Henry reads the boast about the knife as disclosing Buckingham's true 'period': to kill the king. 'Attach'd' means arrested, seized — the legal term for taking a person into custody. Henry passes from dramatic realization ('there's his period') to immediate legal action ('he is attach'd') in a single couplet.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'period' n. 4a: an end, a conclusion, the final point of something; OED s.v. 'attach' v. 5: to seize (a person) by legal authority, to arrest.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 539

OED s.v. 'period' n. 4a records the sense 'an end, conclusion, final point' and s.v. 'attach' v. 5 records the legal sense 'to seize a person by legal authority, to arrest'; both citations are real and directly support the annotation's glosses.

'Period' as end-point or final purpose and 'attach'd' as the legal term for arrest are both standard Elizabethan usages confirmed in OED; the reading of Henry's couplet as moving from dramatic realization to immediate legal action is accurate to the text.

anchor_text: counsellors To Pepin or Clotharius
summary: Pepin (Pépin III, 'the Short,' king of the Franks 751-768) and Clotharius (Clotaire, a recurring name among early Frankish kings) are examples of long-dead ancient French rulers. The Lord Chamberlain mocks the returned courtiers for striking poses so ceremoniously stiff that their very noses seemed to belong to the court of these half-mythic Frankish ancestors rather than to living Englishmen.
detail: Pepin III founded the Carolingian dynasty and was the father of Charlemagne; 'Clotharius' (Clotaire I, d. 561, or Clotaire II, d. 629) was a Merovingian king still further in the past. By invoking these names — ancient, foreign, and faintly ridiculous — the Chamberlain reduces fashionable Francophilia to a pantomime of antique pomposity. The joke lands because the English audience would recognize the names as markers of obsolete French grandeur, precisely the kind of thing a courtier aping French manners might unknowingly invoke. The passage belongs to the play's opening satirical frame, where Norfolk and Buckingham (Act 1.1) and these courtiers ridicule the cultural cost of Henry's continental diplomacy.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1587), on the Frankish kings; the Field of the Cloth of Gold context supplied by the same chronicle.

sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'Pepin' and 'Clotharius': identified as early Frankish monarchs invoked for comic archaism.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 554

Pepin III's dates (751-768), his founding of the Carolingian dynasty, and the Clotaire I/II Merovingian identifications are all accurate; Holinshed covers the Field of the Cloth of Gold context and Schmidt is a real reference.

The Chamberlain's point that stiff French ceremonial poses make their noses look as if they belong to ancient Frankish courts is a straightforward comic reading of 'they keep state so,' and invoking obsolete Frankish kings as markers of risible antique grandeur is mainstream editorial consensus.

anchor_text: new legs, and lame ones. One would take it, That never saw 'em pace before, the spavin Or springhalt reign'd
summary: A spavin is a swelling on a horse's hock joint that causes lameness; a springhalt (also 'stringhalt') is a nervous spasm that makes a horse jerk one hind leg up uncontrollably. Sandys says the returning courtiers have learned such affected new bows and walking-styles from France that a stranger would think a horse disease had broken out among them.
detail: Both spavin and springhalt were recognized equine ailments in the period. The joke is that fashionable new French obeisances and gaits look exactly like the involuntary, jerky movements of a lame horse. 'Legs' means bows (to make a 'leg' was to bow with one leg drawn back); the courtiers' studied French curtsies appear as ungainly twitches. The horse-disease metaphor pairs neatly with Sandys's later 'physic' for the same men (TLN 586-587) and with the play's broader mockery of Francophile affectation.

sources.citation: OED s.v. 'spavin' (a bony or boggy enlargement of a horse's hock) and s.v. 'springhalt' ('stringhalt': a nervous affection causing a horse to jerk up one hind leg when walking).

sources.citation: Onions, C. T. A Shakespeare Glossary (1919), s.v. 'springhalt': 'a disease of horses causing them to jerk up their hind legs.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 556
OED and Onions definitions of spavin (hock-joint swelling causing lameness) and springhalt/stringhalt (nervous spasm causing involuntary hind-leg jerking) are accurate and well-documented.

The horse-disease gloss on affected French bows is standard and well-supported: 'new legs' as 'bows' is established usage, and the equine ailments (spavin, springhalt) map cleanly onto the jerky, involuntary-looking courtly obeisances the passage mocks.

anchor_text: cum privilegio, wear away The lag end of their lewdness
summary: 'Cum privilegio' is Latin for 'with privilege' or 'by special licence' — a formula printed on books to indicate royal or ecclesiastical authorization. Lovell jokes that the banished French gallants may 'with official permission' go somewhere else to work off the dregs ('lag end') of their dissolute habits and be laughed at there. The legal-sounding Latin applied to lewdness is a mock-solemn joke.
detail: The phrase 'cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum' ('with the sole privilege to print') appeared on title pages of licensed publications throughout the sixteenth century. Lovell's use is deliberately incongruous: the state's machinery of censorship and privilege is borrowed to authorize the gallants' residual vice, as if their debauchery has received the royal stamp of approval. 'Lag end' means the last, worst portion (as the tail-end of a piece of cloth). The joke also carries a faint edge: the proclamation reforming the gallants is itself a kind of state instrument, and Lovell quotes a parallel instrument to say it only half-works.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'cum privilegio': the formula 'cum privilegio [regali]' printed on authorized books from the early sixteenth century; s.v. 'lag' adj.: 'last, hindmost, coming at the end.'

sources.citation: Schmidt, Alexander. Shakespeare-Lexicon (1902), s.v. 'lag': 'coming late or last; the lag end = the last or worst part.'

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 584
'Cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum' is a real 16th-century book-licensing formula; OED sense for 'lag' and Schmidt s.v. 'lag' are real references that support the claims.

The mock-solemn application of the printing-licence formula 'cum privilegio' to the gallants' authorized lewdness is a well-attested comic incongruity; 'lag end' as the last, worst portion is straightforward, and the irony that state authority only half-reforms them is squarely in the text.

anchor_text: sly whoresons Have got a speeding trick to lay down ladies
summary: 'To lay down' means to seduce or to get a woman into bed. Lovell pretends to sympathize with the ladies of the court who will 'lose' their French gallants, then undercuts it: the real loss is that those men had an effective technique for getting women to lie down with them. 'Speeding' means fast-working or successful.
detail: The surface meaning is that the ladies will miss the courtiers' company and accomplishments; the bawdy meaning runs underneath the whole speech. 'Lay down ladies' puns on the literal posture of sexual intercourse; 'speeding trick' is the sexual technique that 'speeds' (achieves its end quickly). The A French song and a fiddle (TLN 593) continues the joke: 'fiddle' was slang for sexual activity, and a French song was associated with erotic music. The scene is relaxed, masculine, and mildly ribald — courtiers joking before Wolsey's banquet — in keeping with the play's early comedic register before the tragic falls of Buckingham and Wolsey begin.

sources.name: OED

sources.citation: Williams, Gordon. A Glossary of Shakespeare's Sexual Language (1997), s.v. 'lay': sexual connotation well established by Shakespeare's period.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 591

Williams's Glossary of Shakespeare's Sexual Language (1997) is a real work documenting the sexual sense of 'lay'; OED does record sexual connotations for 'lay' v. and 'speed' v., supporting the bawdy reading.

The bawdy sense of 'lay down' (seduce, get into bed) is well documented in Williams and fits the conversational register; however, the gloss's aside that 'fiddle' was slang for sexual activity slightly overreaches — 'A French song and a fiddle has no fellow' more directly continues the music metaphor from the preceding 'plainsong' exchange, and while 'fiddle' can carry bawdy charge the primary pun here is on French cultural affectation — the core reading remains sound.

anchor_text: honest country lord, as I am, beaten A long time out of play, may bring his plainsong And have an hour of hearing
summary: Sandys contrasts his own simple 'plainsong' with the elaborate French music the gallants have been playing. 'Plainsong' is unadorned medieval church melody — no ornament, no counterpoint, just a single tune — but Sandys uses it to mean his straightforward, old-fashioned English wooing. 'Out of play' means excluded from the game (of courtship), and 'an hour of hearing' means a chance to be listened to by the ladies.
detail: Sandys sets himself up as the honest but outcompeted English suitor, kept 'out of play' — a sporting metaphor — by the glamour of the returned French gallants. 'Plainsong' was the ancient liturgical chant of the Church (Latin: cantus planus), proverbially simple and unadorned; here it becomes a mock-modest term for Sandys's unembellished courting style. 'Held current music too' (TLN 599) means 'accepted as genuine and in fashion as well' — his plain tune was once coin of the realm. The Chamberlain's reply ('Your colt's tooth is not cast yet') shows he reads the speech entirely as a boast about Sandys's continuing sexual appetite.

OED 'plainsong' (unadorned church melody used figuratively) and Onions 'plain-song' and 'out of play' are real entries that accurately support the claims made.

The contrast between Sandys's unadorned 'plainsong' courting and the French gallants' elaborate arts is directly supported by the text and the Chamberlain's immediate reply about the 'colt's tooth'; reading 'out of play' as a sporting-exclusion metaphor and 'held current music' as 'accepted as genuine coin' are both defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: Your colt's tooth is not cast yet
summary: A colt's milk-tooth falls out when the horse matures; a man whose 'colt's tooth is not cast' still has the frisky, lecherous desires of a young stallion, even in old age. The Lord Chamberlain teases Sandys that his appetite for women has not faded with age. Sandys's reply — 'Nor shall not, while I have a stump' — coarsens the joke: a stump of a tooth, but also bawdily a stump of something else.
detail: The proverb 'to have a colt's tooth' for an old man's lingering lechery was current by the late sixteenth century. Chaucer uses the image in the Wife of Bath's Prologue ('I hadde a coltes tooth'). In horsemanship the shedding of the milk-teeth marks the horse's transition from colt to mature animal; a horse that does not cast them on schedule is proverbially still young and unruly in temperament. Sandys's 'stump' extends the dental image into sexual innuendo — a stump of a tooth, yes, but also the blunt remainder of a decayed or broken member, implying he can still make some use of it. The exchange is the scene's most concentrated piece of bawdy by-play, consistent with the loose, convivial tone before the banquet.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'colt's-tooth': 'the wanton or unruly disposition of a young man; lascivious inclinations' (first citation Chaucer, Wife of Bath's Prologue, l. 602).

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 601

OED 'colt's-tooth' is a real entry for lascivious old-man disposition; the Chaucer citation (Wife of Bath's Prologue, l. 602 — 'But yet I hadde alwey a coltes tooth') is accurate in both text and line number.

The proverbial 'colt's tooth' for an old man's lingering lechery is solidly attested (Chaucer, OED), the dental/sexual double meaning of 'stump' is an obvious extension that editors uniformly accept, and the exchange is entirely consistent with the scene's ribald male-bonding register.

anchor_text: spoke to, with Sir Henry Guildford, This night to be comptrollers
summary: A comptroller (also 'controller') of a household or feast was the officer responsible for overseeing the accounts and practical management of the entertainment — checking expenses, supervising the stewards, and keeping order. The Lord Chamberlain and Sir Henry Guildford have been appointed to run Wolsey's banquet that night.
detail: The office of Comptroller of the Household was one of the great offices of the royal court, ranking just below the Treasurer. At a grand supper like Wolsey's, being named a comptroller meant being responsible for the whole management of the feast — a mark of trust and responsibility. Sir Henry Guildford (the character named here) was a real officer: he appears in Act 1.4 welcoming the guests to the banquet, and historically served as Master of the Revels and a courtier close to Henry. The detail grounds the transition to the next scene (1.4) by establishing that the Lord Chamberlain and Guildford will both be present at the feast where the king first dances with Anne Bullen.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'comptroller' (also 'controller'): 'an officer who checks the accounts and superintends the management of a household, estate, or public institution.'

The definition of comptroller as the feast-management officer and the identification of Sir Henry Guildford as a historical figure who appears in 1.4 are accurate and well-grounded; the note that this detail bridges to the next scene is a sound structural observation.

anchor_text: noble bevy, has brought with her
summary: 'Bevy' is an archaic collective noun originally applied to a flock of larks or a company of ladies. Guildford uses it as a courtly compliment meaning 'this fine company of women.' The word carries a suggestion of light, fluttering charm rather than anything derogatory.

OED 'bevy, n.' for a company of ladies, quails, or larks with 15th-century first attestation is confirmed; Onions' Shakespeare Glossary is a genuine reference.
'Bevy' as a collective for ladies is well-attested and the reading that it is a courtly compliment rather than derogatory is defensible and mainstream.

anchor_text: lay thoughts in him, some of these / Should find a running banquet
summary: A 'running banquet' was a light, impromptu feast served informally (as opposed to a formal seated dinner). Sandys says that if the Cardinal shared his 'lay' (non-clerical, worldly) thoughts, some of the ladies would find themselves getting a running banquet before they rested — meaning a hurried, rushed 'treat.' The phrase carries an obvious sexual innuendo: informal appetites quickly satisfied.
detail: The joke turns on the contrast between Wolsey's celibate Cardinal dignity and the frankly predatory lust Sandys attributes to his own 'lay' (secular) mind. 'Lay' puns on layperson vs. the act of lying with someone. The speech establishes Sandys immediately as the scene's bawdy comic voice before his confessor-penance exchange with Lovell makes the double entendre even more explicit.

anchor_text: were but now confessor / To one or two of these
summary: The exchange between Lovell and Sandys plays on the Catholic practice of auricular confession, where a priest (confessor) hears a penitent's sins and assigns penance. anchor_text: they speak no English, thus they pray'd / To tell your Grace, that, having heard by fame / Of this so noble and so fair assembly
summary: The arrival of the king and his party disguised as shepherds who 'speak no English' is a standard masque convention. In an Elizabethan or Jacobean court masque, noble or royal performers entered in costume and persona, often posing as foreigners or mythological figures, while a spokesperson explained their fictional purpose. The fiction of not speaking English lets the host respond ceremonially without acknowledging the obvious identity of the masquers.
detail: The masque was the prestige entertainment form of the Jacobean court (Ben Jonson wrote masques for James I). Its conventions — disguise, the fictional journey to a court 'heard of by fame,' the choice of a dance partner — were recognizable to the audience. The king's choice of shepherd costume echoes the pastoral masque tradition in which royalty donned the costume of humble figures (an established topos of royal humility and mythologized simplicity). Historically, Henry VIII was known for exactly this kind of surprise unmasking entertainment; Holinshed records similar revels. The scene closely follows George Cavendish's eyewitness account in his Life of Wolsey.

anchor_text: Came to the bar; where to his accusations
summary: 'The bar' was the physical barrier in a law court behind which a prisoner stood to be charged. anchor_text: was not one Doctor Pace In this man's place before him

anchor_text: two reverend cardinal virtues; But cardinal sins and hollow hearts I fear ye
summary: Katherine builds an extended pun on the word 'cardinal.' In Christian theology the four cardinal virtues are prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance; the seven deadly sins are sometimes called cardinal sins. She had hoped the men before her were 'reverend cardinal virtues' — holy men embodying the virtues of their rank. Instead she suspects them of 'cardinal sins,' which are also, literally, sins committed by cardinals. The pun is bitter and exact.
detail: The adjective 'cardinal' (from Latin cardo, a hinge) meant 'of chief importance' — hence both the theological cardinal virtues (the four on which good conduct hinges) and the Church office of Cardinal (the hinges on whom Rome's governance turns). By playing 'cardinal virtues' against 'cardinal sins' in consecutive lines, Katherine exposes the gap between what princes of the Church ought to embody and what Wolsey and Campeius are doing in her apartments. The wordplay was conventional enough that an Elizabethan audience would catch it immediately; the theological precision makes it cutting rather than merely clever.

anchor_text: I dare not make myself so guilty, To give up willingly that noble title Your master wed me to. Nothing but death Shall e'er divorce my dignities
summary: Katherine refuses to voluntarily surrender her title of Queen of England. She argues that to accept the divorce would make her an accomplice to her own wrong — 'guilty' of abandoning a lawful marriage. The phrase 'nothing but death shall e'er divorce my dignities' is the scene's moral climax and its most famous single line. Historically Katherine maintained her title and refused to call herself anything but Queen until her death in 1536.

Her stance had international implications — as long as she claimed to be the lawful queen, any child born of Anne Bullen was a bastard in the eyes of Catholic Europe and of Henry's own kingdom. Her position also challenged the royal supremacy over the Church: if the Pope's dispensation that made the marriage lawful was valid, no English authority could undo it. She was right in canon law; she simply lost the political battle.

anchor_text: The hearts of princes kiss obedience, So much they love it; but to stubborn spirits They swell, and grow as terrible as storms

The 'bright exhalation' is especially poignant for Wolsey: brilliant, swift, and self-consuming, visible to all but vanishing without trace.

anchor_text: Fall into the compass of a praemunire

The threat of praemunire against the entire Church of England (1531) was a lever forcing the clergy to recognize royal supremacy; Wolsey's personal indictment in 1529 was the dress rehearsal. The forfeitures meant that everything he owned — York Place, the Hampton Court building works, his plate, his books — became the Crown's.

summary: The anointing with holy oil and the crown of St Edward the Confessor were the two most sacred acts of an English coronation. The 'bird of peace' is a dove, the top ornament of the sovereign's orb or sceptre.
detail: Edward the Confessor (reigned 1042-1066) was the sainted Anglo-Saxon king who rebuilt Westminster Abbey, where he was buried and venerated. His crown and regalia became the symbolic link connecting every subsequent English monarch to the pre-Conquest Anglo-Saxon tradition, lending them sacred authority that transcended dynastic changes. The anointing with holy oil (chrism) was the sacramental heart of the coronation, understood to mark the king or queen as God's anointed — the same theological point that makes regicide a quasi-sacrilege in Richard II and throughout the histories. The dove on the sovereign's rod signified peace and the Holy Spirit. The Third Gentleman's list authenticates the scene with precise ceremonial detail drawn from Holinshed.

anchor_text: Together sung "Te Deum."
summary: The 'Te Deum' is an ancient Latin hymn of praise and thanksgiving ('We praise thee, O God'), traditionally sung at the conclusion of a coronation and on other great public occasions. Singing it marked the ceremony's completion and gave the whole event a religious ratification.
detail: The Te Deum Laudamus (Latin: 'We praise you, God') dates from the fourth or fifth century and was one of the fixed canticles of the daily office in the medieval church. For Shakespeare's audience in 1613, still within living memory of the Reformation, the Latin Te Deum was associated with pre-Reformation ceremonial — though an English version was included in the Book of Common Prayer (1549 onward). The fact that the scene does not flinch at describing a pre-Reformation Latin coronation rite reflects the play's deliberately unpolemical handling of religious change. The term was current enough that the audience would have recognized it as the climactic hymn without needing explanation.

anchor_text: You must no more call it York Place, that's past; For, since the Cardinal fell, that title's lost. 'Tis now the King's, and call'd Whitehall.
summary: York Place was the official London residence of the Archbishop of York — but Wolsey had transformed it into a palace rivaling the royal palaces. When Henry stripped Wolsey of his offices in 1529, he also seized York Place and renamed it Whitehall. It became the principal royal palace for the next 170 years and gave its name to the street that still runs past the Palace of Westminster.

Henry's seizure of it after Wolsey's fall (1529) was a sign of how completely the King claimed the fruits of his minister's rise: Anne Bullen was installed there while still a royal mistress. Whitehall Palace (destroyed by fire in 1698) was the main royal residence for the Tudor and early Stuart monarchs; the Banqueting House of 1622, the only surviving fragment, stands on the site today. The First Gentleman's correction is both a piece of topography and a reminder of Wolsey's ruin: the Cardinal's name has been erased from his greatest monument.

anchor_text: Stokesly and Gardiner; the one of Winchester, Newly preferr'd from the King's secretary
summary: The two bishops flanking Anne are both men who served Henry's religious policy but represent different factions. His enmity with Cranmer (already signaled here at TLN 2389-91) is the subject of Act 5. John Stokesley (1475-1539), Bishop of London from 1530, canvassed European universities for opinions supporting Henry's annulment. Together they embody the unstable alliance between royal supremacy and Catholic theology that the Reformation would shatter within a generation. The Third Gentleman's noting of Gardiner's recent promotion ('Newly preferr'd') anticipates his rising importance.

anchor_text: Thomas Cromwell; A man in much esteem with the King, and truly A worthy friend. The King has made him master O' the jewel house, And one, already, of the privy council.
summary: Thomas Cromwell (c. 1485-1540) was Wolsey's secretary and rose, after his master's fall, to become the king's chief minister. 'Master of the Jewel House' was a royal household office responsible for the crown's plate and treasures; a seat on the Privy Council was real power. The Third Gentleman's confident prediction that Cromwell 'will deserve more' is ironic: he rose to be Earl of Essex before being executed in 1540.

He served as Master of the Jewel House from 1532, joined the Privy Council in 1531, became Lord Privy Seal (1536), and eventually Earl of Essex (1540) before being beheaded on a charge of treason and heresy. In Henry VIII the play he appears in his rising phase, his later ruin and execution outside the play's action. The Third Gentleman's admiring characterization ('worthy friend') and his confident prediction of Cromwell's future greatness are delivered in dramatic irony, since the play's first audience knew how both men ended.

anchor_text: the great child of honour, Cardinal Wolsey, Was dead
summary: 'Child of honour' is Katherine's ironic epithet for Wolsey. A 'child of honour' is someone born into, or formed by, honour — but Wolsey was born the son of an Ipswich butcher, not a nobleman. Katherine names him this at the moment of his death, implying he was honour's creation even if not honour's offspring — and leaving the irony open.

'Child of honour' is thus simultaneously elevated language (fit for the dead) and a veiled reminder of his low origins. Katherine uses it coolly, not mockingly — she is a queen observing the proprieties of speaking well of the recently dead even as she prepares to speak ill of him.

anchor_text: the stout Earl Northumberland Arrested him at York
summary: In November 1530 Henry Percy, 6th Earl of Northumberland, rode to Cawood Castle near York and arrested the fallen Wolsey for high treason under a writ of praemunire (asserting papal authority within the realm). Wolsey was too ill to travel fast and never reached London; he died at Leicester Abbey in November 1530. Griffith's account follows the historical record closely.
detail: The arrest capped a dramatic fall: Wolsey had surrendered the Great Seal in October 1529, been stripped of his offices, and retreated northward hoping to govern his diocese of York and rebuild royal favor. Henry Percy had, years earlier, been forbidden by Wolsey himself from marrying Anne Boleyn — so the Earl's role as Wolsey's arresting officer carries historical irony. The main source is George Cavendish's eyewitness memoir, which gives a detailed, sympathetic account of the Cardinal's last journey and death at Leicester.

Leicester Abbey was dissolved in 1538; the site is now lost, and Wolsey has no marked grave.

anchor_text: He gave his honours to the world again, His blessed part to heaven
summary: Griffith describes a good Christian death in two movements: giving back earthly titles ('honours') to the world — relinquishing all worldly rank — and surrendering the soul ('his blessed part') to God. The formula reflects the standard Elizabethan theology of dying well: a peaceful death required letting go of wealth and position and dying in repentance.

Griffith's eulogy specifically satisfies all the checklist items — Wolsey died in 'full of repentance, / Continual meditations, tears, and sorrows' — and the two-part formula ('honours to the world / blessed part to heaven') enacts the separation of the temporal from the eternal that a good death required. This is the mirror image of the 'naked to mine enemies' speech in 3.2, where Wolsey first achieves this renunciation.

anchor_text: Simony was fair-play
summary: Simony is the buying and selling of church offices, appointments, or spiritual goods for money — named after Simon Magus, who in the Bible tried to buy the gift of the Holy Spirit from the apostles. Katherine's charge is that Wolsey treated it as normal business. It was a canonical crime for which the Church repeatedly condemned its own clergy throughout the medieval and Tudor periods.

As a cardinal, Lord Chancellor, and the king's chief minister simultaneously, Wolsey held extraordinary ecclesiastical and temporal patronage — he could effectively appoint bishops and abbots — and the charges of simony against him were widespread and credible. Katherine's indictment here follows the accusations laid by his enemies and reflected in Hall and Holinshed.

summary: Griffith acknowledges Wolsey's low birth — his father was an Ipswich butcher — while arguing he was shaped for greatness from birth. His enemies never let him forget his origins; his defenders (like Griffith here) argued his genius transcended them.

anchor_text: Those twins of learning that he rais'd in you, Ipswich and Oxford! one of which fell with him
summary: Wolsey founded two colleges: Cardinal College at Ipswich (his birthplace, 1528) and Cardinal College at Oxford (1525, later refounded as Christ Church). When he fell in 1529, Ipswich College was immediately dissolved and its endowments seized. Oxford survived because Henry VIII re-endowed it, and it remains one of Oxford's most prominent colleges today. Griffith calls them 'twins of learning' because both were founded in the same burst of patronage in the late 1520s.

Oxford's Cardinal College was refounded by Henry VIII as King Henry VIII's College (1532) and again as Christ Church (1546). Griffith notes that the Oxford college remained 'still so rising' — it was already famous enough that 'Christendom shall ever speak his virtue.' The contrast between the demolished Ipswich foundation and the surviving Oxford one dramatizes the mixed legacy Griffith is describing: some of Wolsey's good works endured, some fell with him.

anchor_text: His overthrow heap'd happiness upon him; For then, and not till then, he felt himself, And found the blessedness of being little

anchor_text: that sad note I nam'd my knell, whilst I sit meditating On that celestial harmony I go to
summary: Katherine asks for the piece of sad music she has already chosen as her 'knell' — the bell rung to announce a death. She meditates on the 'celestial harmony' she is about to join: the music of the spheres, the ancient idea that the planets and stars produced a perfect, inaudible music as they moved. The earthly music is a dim echo of what she is moving toward.

Shakespeare returns to this idea in The Merchant of Venice (5.1: 'There's not the smallest orb... but in his motion like an angel sings') and Pericles (5.1, where Diana appears to heavenly music). Katherine's vision of angels bringing garlands (the staged Vision) immediately follows this speech and gives the celestial harmony a theatrical shape.

anchor_text: The model of our chaste loves, his young daughter
summary: 'Model' here means image, likeness, or embodiment — not a miniature or a person who models clothes. Katherine calls the princess Mary the living image ('model') of her and Henry's lawful, chaste marriage. The word carried the sense of 'pattern' or 'representation' in Elizabethan English.
detail: The 'young daughter' is Princess Mary (born 1516, later Mary I), Katherine's only surviving child. At the time of Katherine's death in 1536 Mary was nineteen, had been declared illegitimate by Act of Parliament, and had been removed from the succession. Katherine's letter in the historical record pleads for Mary's restoration to favor; the play's 'model of our chaste loves' encapsulates in a phrase both the legitimacy of the marriage (chaste = lawful, not adulterous) and Mary's status as its proof.

sources.name: OED
sources.citation: OED s.v. 'model' n. 5: 'a representation, image, or embodiment' — Elizabethan usage that precedes the modern sense of a physical small-scale copy.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
sources.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Katherine's last letter and her plea for her daughter's recognition.
